P01.passage: In 1894 a court ruled on a strike by a port city's dockworkers' union, which then had four thousand members and a hall near the docks. The court held the union an unlawful conspiracy and ordered its strike fund repaid to the men who had paid into it and its hall sold. At a final meeting the members voted without dissent to comply, and the hall was sold that month. No dockworkers' union met in the city again until 1919. Writing fifty years later, one labor historian concluded that the ruling had, in effect, ______ the union.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: A gravel bar a mile long runs from the southern shore of a bay toward an island at the bay's mouth. At the lowest tides its crest lies dry from the shore to the island for two hours, and at high water eight feet of water covers it from end to end. The town's sheep graze the island's pasture from May to October. The fishing fleet sails over the bar at any point along its length on the flood, and winter swells run across it into the bay. One historian of the bay's fishing town wrote that the bar had served the town above all as its ______.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: In 1980 a storm dropped a two-hundred-year-old fir into a mountain stream, and its trunk, four feet thick, has lain there ever since. It came to rest along the current, parallel to the banks, and floods sweeping around it have scoured a pool ten feet deep in its shade. Each summer adult salmon on their way upstream gather in the pool by the hundreds, each staying a few days before going on to gravel beds miles above. Every winter the flood that deepens the pool runs over the trunk. After a decade of watching it, one ecologist called the log, above all, the valley's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. All the ore came out through one mine head, and from the town the slopes and the summit cairn of 1885 look as they do in old photographs. Since 1975 a road on the north slope has dropped a foot, a spring on the east slope has vanished into the ground, and two farmhouses on the south slope have been abandoned when their floors split. Trout still rise in the streams below. Surveying the mountain in 1980, one geologist wrote that mining had ______ it.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: A potter fired a batch of white bowls painted with blue brushwork under a clear glaze. When the kiln was opened, the brushwork could be made out only faintly, as though seen through frost, while the white of each bowl looked even whiter than before. Under a fingertip the glaze was as smooth as glass, and a week later the bowls had held tea without a mark. In her notes on the batch, the potter concluded that the firing had ______ the glaze.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: A sand spit four miles long curves across a lagoon's mouth, with a lighthouse near its hooked tip and a road along its crest. In 1953 a three-day gale drove waves over the crest. When the water fell, the crest's loose sand was gone, and the road ran over a bed of fist-sized cobbles that had lain beneath it. The next week the keeper drove that road past the lighthouse to the hooked tip. In the next twenty winters the spit lost less ground than in any twenty on record. Comparing surveys made before and after that winter, one geologist concluded that the gale had ______ the spit.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: A cave high in a cliff overlooks a ford where reindeer herds crossed a river each spring and autumn fourteen thousand years ago; its back chamber stays near freezing all year. Excavators found that chamber's floor ringed with hearths, layer above layer, all from the winter months after the autumn herds had gone south. Among the hearths lay grass bedding, stone scrapers for working hides and milk teeth shed by children. From the finds, one archaeologist concluded that the valley's hunters used the cave above all as their ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Sailing in twenty years later, surveyors found the old sea caves in the eastern cliffs standing nine meters above the tide, while at the western end the village's quays lay under the harbor at high water. The farms between were planted as before, their stone walls and orchards where the 1880 chart had placed them. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water burst through a failed levee in a current strong enough to roll boulders and was gone within hours. Behind it last year's stubble had vanished, the crust lay broken into slabs turned on edge, and the pale sandy soil beneath was heaped in long ridges running downstream, with furrows between them. The farmers then sowed the same seed wheat into the furrows. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. Crews could no longer hold fish back in their ice holds for a better price, and buyers from the inland towns began coming to the quay every morning, not just after a big catch. Within two years the inland fish shops, which had chalked up new prices daily, were printing their price lists once a season. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. Governments of the farm party raised the rate and governments of the city party cut it, and the two held office by turns, so six changes were rises and five were cuts, each undoing the one before. Two of the rises came in years of record wheat prices. In 1950 the rate stood within a cent of its first level, and the neighboring countries left their own duties untouched all century. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: Between 1925 and 1935 a record company sent engineers into a mountain region to record its fiddlers and ballad singers, and it sold the records by the thousand. In the studio the engineers had the fiddlers retune to standard pitch and paired every singer with a hired guitarist, and singers who heard their own records began to drop the slides and cracks from their voices. They still sang every verse of the old ballads, at dances and on porches all over the region. Looking back in 1970, one folklorist argued that the records had ______ the region's songs.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: From 1950 to 1990, scientists studied one small, deep, cold lake in a northern forest more closely than any other lake in the region, and its bottom mud lies in fine yearly layers. The layers are thick in wet years and thin in dry ones, and cores of them gave the region its only year-by-year record of rainfall back to the last ice age. The shrimp and plankton in its water are those of every lake nearby. In a history of that work, one scientist called the lake, for those four decades, above all the region's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. The wire service soon sold its bulletins to the new radio stations as well, and by 1940 the stations read each day's main stories aloud at noon; the papers, printed at dawn, carried those stories a day after listeners had heard them. Circulation and advertising kept rising, as readers bought the papers for the local news and detail that radio had no time for. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. The road's only water for nine days lay in its wells, and a fort of the river kingdom stood over them. Every caravan paid a tenth of its load to water there, the year round, and caravans of the kingdom's enemies were turned back. The rest of each load went on to the coast unopened. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. Its springs held up, and in the eighth week canoes still ran the whole river from the springs to the lake, floating over riffles where in other dry summers they had to be carried. Along the shallow, treeless lower miles, biologists counted thousands of dead trout in water that ran fast and clear. In the shaded upper miles near the cold springs, the trout lived. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. The road was laid along the river's far bank, its nearest exit nine miles away. Trucks that had crawled down the main street took the new road, and the mill, which shipped by rail, kept its orders and workers. By 1990 the town still had nearly eight thousand people, the families of 1958 still ran most of its forty stores, and its newest building was the 1951 post office. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there is thin and clear, and a film of algae grows on its underside wherever light comes through. Late in winter, when the open water beyond holds almost no plankton, krill crowd beneath it to graze the film, cod follow them, and ringed seals hunt the cod from breathing holes kept open in the ice. When the ice breaks up and drifts out to sea in spring, the krill stay behind. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. The restorers took the varnish off with strong solvents in a few weeks, working past the smoke into the paint itself, and in places the thin glazes that had modeled the saints' faces came away on the swabs, leaving flat pink underpaint. The oak panels went back into the frame as they had come out, and the altarpiece was hung that spring. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. The village versions recorded around 1900 kept all eleven episodes and the desert capital, and took as long to tell as the printed text took to read. Tellers had reworked every line of them: the son's three tricks now came in rising order, the riddle rhymed, and the surprise that the printed text gave away midway now fell on the last line. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: A rocky island a quarter mile long lies in the middle of a wide river where it crosses a farming valley. On either side the channel is too deep to wade at any season. When gales blow down the valley, barges from the whole river tie up along its downwind shore, where the water lies deep and still. Raiders coming downriver in 1640 moored there too while they burned the valley's farms, and the spring floods that spread over the valley floor cover the island as well. In a history of the valley, one historian called the island, above all, the valley's ______.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. Its four shrines stand in the city temple's order, and the dragons over its gate match the city temple's at a third the size. One of them even repeats the chipped claw that a city carver left by accident on his dragon. It has never had monks; the farming families who keep it still walk to the city each spring for the great festival. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: In 1965 a carmaker from abroad opened a plant outside a port city, on a site its board had chosen after two years of study. The company already owned two large factories inland, bought from a local maker in 1960. The new plant, a plain shed beside the port's rail yard, built a few hundred cars a year, and every engineer and foreman the company hired in the country spent two years on its line before moving inland, where by 1980 they ran both factories. In a history of the company, one economist called the plant, above all, its ______ in the country.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: In 1952, after three dry years, a river broke its banks and spread for five days across a broad valley, filling every side channel between its villages and their fields. It had passed through a chain of mountain lakes on its way down and ran clear, and when it drained the farmers found their ditches and field boundaries as they had left them. Winter wheat sown into the wet ground that week came up thick on every flooded farm, while on the terraces above the valley it withered for a fourth year. One agronomist later argued that, for the farmers, the flood had above all ______ their fields.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. The lake lies on porous limestone, and water seeps through its floor into caverns that drain toward another valley. In most months the river leaves it at half its inflow and in dry summers not at all, and what flow there is comes off the top of a lake the seepage keeps shallow, so in August the ponds draw on wells. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay and a row of warehouses, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. A hook of rock closes a deep bay on its landward side, and a lighthouse on the hook shows the way in. When winter gales blew down the strait, ships bound for the cities ran into the bay and waited, landing perishable cargo in the warehouses until they sailed; in calm weather they passed the island on either side. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. Its staff crossed the district's wheat with hardy strains from abroad, and each autumn they handed a sack of that year's cross to any farmer who asked. By 1950 nearly every field in the district had been sown from those sacks, and seed that farmers saved and passed to neighbors had carried the crosses into three adjoining counties. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: A cave opens in the side of a limestone hill above a village, and its passages wind back for a mile under the hill. It has no other opening. For hours before a storm, wind blows out of its mouth hard enough to flatten the grass, and for hours after the storm passes it blows back in. The drips from its roof gather into a brook that runs out of the mouth, and its air is the same mild temperature winter and summer. In a survey of the district, one geologist called the cave, above all, the hill's ______.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: A canal dug in the 1300s runs for two miles beside the old center of a river city. Barges carried grain, coal and building stone up it from the river, and the warehouses of the city's merchant guild lined both its banks to the water's edge. Tanneries and dye works emptied into it along its length, and tolls on its barges were the largest item in the city's revenue. In her history of the city, one historian called the canal, above all, the city's ______.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: In 1987 a plowman near an old river landing turned up a clay pot buried around the year 900, holding some nine hundred silver coins and pieces of cut silver. The coins come from a dozen ports along the coast, and twelve different owners' marks are scratched into the cut silver. The pot lay in a boat shed at the landing that, a nearby abbey's chronicle records, a trading crew of twelve shared each winter. From its contents, one archaeologist concluded that the hoard had been, above all, its owners' ______.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: In a pond where half the snails carry a parasitic worm that matures inside ducks, a biologist kept infected and uninfected snails side by side for three years, in tanks and in a pen with feeding ducks. Infected snails laid no eggs at all and grew a third larger than the others, living just as long. Ducks in the pen took the two kinds at the same rate, and a bacterium that swept the tanks in the second summer killed both kinds alike. From these results, she concluded that the worm had, above all, ______ its host.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, icy bodies that drifted near it were thrown onto long, stretched paths, most of them clean out of the system, and the belt lost half its members in the first hundred million years. The few hurled inward struck the rocky planets about as often as icy bodies did in the run without the giant. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Stoats from both woods came into the hedge on most winter nights, each working a few hundred yards of the bank, and went back before dawn to the wood it had come from. By late winter most of the burrows stood empty, and in summer, when voles were plentiful in the woods, collared stoats hardly came near the hedge. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: In 1838 a merchant inherited an estate of farms and oak woods worked by hired hands, and his account books for the next twenty years survive. In 1841 they record a sum from a naval shipyard larger than ten years of the estate's profits. The next year comes the pay of extra men hired to pull stumps and sow grass, while the regular hands' wages run on unchanged to 1858. From those books, one historian concluded that, above all, he had ______ the estate.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: Between the two world wars, exiles working for their small homeland's independence gathered at a café in a foreign capital, where the owner kept the back room for them. The movement had split into three parties, each with its own offices and newspaper elsewhere in the city, and foreign reporters went to those offices for statements. Members of all three came to the café, where news from home passed from table to table, and party leaders who would not share a platform met over chess in the back room. In a memoir of those years, one journalist called the café, more than anything, the movement's ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: A chalk quarry worked out in the 1800s lies at the edge of a market town, a pit two hundred yards across with galleries cut back into its walls. A ramp runs down to its dry, level floor, and its walls are sheer on every other side. Every Saturday since 1880 farmers from three valleys have driven their carts down the ramp, and the town's grocers buy most of their week's stock on its floor. The galleries run only a few yards into the chalk, and the farmers stable their horses in them. One local historian has called the quarry, above all, the town's ______.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: In 1904 a new firm began making typewriters in a country where one older company had sold nearly every machine for thirty years, and by 1914 the newcomer was outselling it. Its first machine typed with an electric motor, a feature the older company had dismissed as a toy, and shared not one part with the older company's model. Both firms sold through the same dealers, and the older company's mechanical machines, unchanged, lost buyers every year. Reading both firms' records, one historian concluded that the newcomer had above all ______ its rival.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. When the staff returned, the rare-book room was untouched; whole floors of bound newspapers, old textbooks and duplicate copies stood empty, about a third of the collection by weight. The ledgers of the occupation's paper ministry, short of stock for its own printing, list the library as a source of two hundred tons. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: In 1897 gold was found in the hills above a small river town, and the rush lasted six years. The diggings lay a day's ride up a valley to the east, and within two years a road ran there from the town's back street, where new stores and a bank opened facing it. The river landing, the town's trading place since 1840, fell idle. After 1903 a railway took the road's route east to timber, and by 1920 the town, still about eight hundred people, did its trade along the old back street. Looking back in 1920, one historian wrote that the gold rush had ______ the town.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: In 1590 the council of a river city built a stone granary on its market square, large enough to hold a year's grain for every household. The lords of the villages around it often quarreled with the city over its barge tolls. Each autumn the council bought every village's surplus at harvest prices, and each spring it shipped the grain downriver to whichever port paid most, in famine years as in good. The city raised no hearth tax except in the two years a war closed the river. One economic historian has argued that for two centuries the granary served above all as the city's ______.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
